title: CosMAP: Contrastive Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimensionality Reduction of Omics and Genealogical Data
summary: Omics datasets, particularly single-cell RNA sequencing data, are high-dimensional, sparse, noisy, and dominated by zero values, making faithful low-dimensional representation challenging. Existing dimensionality-reduction methods may distort local neighbourhoods, global organization, or the cohesion of meaningful populations, with similar limitations arising in genealogical data. We introduce Contrastive Manifold Approximation and Projection (CosMAP), a graph-based unsupervised dimensionality-reduction method for producing faithful and interpretable embeddings. CosMAP extends the graph-based framework of UMAP by combining cosine-similarity neighbourhoods with temperature-normalized contrastive affinities, which are optimized in the embedding space using an attractive--repulsive objective. It further employs a two-phase refinement strategy: an intermediate higher-dimensional representation is first learned and then used to reconstruct the neighbourhood graph and initialize the final low-dimensional embedding. We evaluate CosMAP on MNIST and USPS handwritten-digit datasets, mouse retina and cortex single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets, and a large genealogical kinship dataset derived from BALSAC-CARTaGENE. Compared with state-of-the-art dimensionality-reduction methods, CosMAP produces more coherent visual representations, improves neighbourhood preservation, and provides clearer global organization of digit classes, biological cell populations, and regional genealogical patterns. These results indicate that CosMAP offers a robust framework for exploratory analysis of complex, sparse, high-dimensional data. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/FenosoaRandrianjatovo/CosMAP-dr.

AI.tldr: CosMAP is a graph-based unsupervised dimensionality-reduction method that extends UMAP by combining cosine-similarity neighborhoods with temperature-normalized contrastive affinities and a two-phase refinement strategy, producing more coherent and faithful embeddings for high-dimensional, sparse omics and genealogical data.
AI.motivation: Omics datasets, especially single-cell RNA sequencing data, are high-dimensional, sparse, noisy, and zero-dominated, making faithful low-dimensional representation difficult. Existing dimensionality-reduction methods distort local neighborhoods, global organization, or population cohesion, and similar issues arise in genealogical data.
AI.method: CosMAP extends UMAP's graph-based framework by using cosine-similarity neighborhoods with temperature-normalized contrastive affinities, optimized in embedding space via an attractive-repulsive objective. It employs a two-phase refinement: first learning an intermediate higher-dimensional representation, then using it to reconstruct the neighborhood graph and initialize the final low-dimensional embedding.
AI.result: Evaluated on MNIST, USPS, mouse retina and cortex scRNA-seq datasets, and BALSAC-CARTaGENE genealogical kinship data, CosMAP outperforms state-of-the-art methods by producing more coherent visual representations, better neighborhood preservation, and clearer global organization of digit classes, biological cell populations, and regional genealogical patterns.
AI.conclusion: CosMAP provides a robust framework for exploratory analysis of complex, sparse, high-dimensional data, with implementation publicly available.

title: Consciousness as Intrinsic Structure: Towards a Chemistry of Experience
summary: To be conscious is to have an experience - not a collection of phenomenal atoms, but a structured whole composed of distinctions and the relations that bind them. Integrated Information Theory (IIT) identifies the essential properties of every experience (axioms), formulates them operationally as postulates that a substrate must satisfy, and unfolds the cause-effect power of the resulting complex into a $Φ$-structure. Accounting for a content of experience is then a matter of identifying the phenomenal distinctions and relations that compose it, and showing them reflected one-to-one in the causal distinctions and relations of the corresponding $Φ$-structure. We apply that method to three pervasive contents whose structure is partly open to introspection. Spatial extendedness is composed of spots, whose elemental signature is reflexivity, bound by reflexive inclusion, connection, and fusion; temporal flow is composed of moments, whose signature is directedness, bound by directed inclusion, connection, and fusion; objects bind a particular configuration of features to a general concept through relations bearing the signature of hierarchy. The endeavor is akin to chemistry, which accounts for an endless variety of compounds from a limited set of elements and the ways they bond. We assess these accounts against seven criteria of a good explanation - scope, synthesis, specificity, self-consistency, system consistency, simplicity, and scientific validation - and sketch the prediction that follows: altering the structure specified by a substrate should alter the corresponding content, even when activity and behavior are held comparable. The same method may reach narrow qualia, which resist introspection, and the compound contents that bind many qualia together, though there it remains a proof of concept and an open research program.

AI.tldr: This paper applies Integrated Information Theory (IIT) to explain the structure of conscious experience—spatial extendedness, temporal flow, and objects—by mapping phenomenal distinctions and relations onto causal distinctions and relations in Φ-structures, then evaluating these accounts against seven explanatory criteria and outlining testable predictions.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to move beyond abstract axioms of IIT by demonstrating how its framework can concretely account for the structural content of experience, addressing pervasive phenomenal features whose introspective structure is partially accessible.
AI.method: The paper applies IIT's method: identify essential axioms of experience, operationalize them as postulates for a substrate, unfold the cause-effect power into a Φ-structure, and establish one-to-one correspondences between phenomenal distinctions/relations and causal distinctions/relations in the Φ-structure. It then assesses these accounts using seven criteria of a good explanation.
AI.result: The accounts map spatial extendedness to reflexive spots bound by inclusion/connection/fusion relations, temporal flow to directed moments bound by similar relations, and objects to hierarchical relations binding features to concepts. These are evaluated against seven quality criteria, yielding a falsifiable prediction: altering substrate structure alters content even when activity and behavior are comparable.
AI.conclusion: IIT provides a principled, chemistry-like framework for explaining structured experience. While applications to narrow qualia and compound contents remain a proof of concept, the approach offers a systematically testable research program for consciousness science.

title: Large-scale AI-Ready Data for Anti-Cancer Drug Response Modeling
summary: Drug response prediction (DRP) models are an active area of research in pharmacogenomics, with growing potential to accelerate the identification of effective anticancer drugs. However, their predictive performance is often constrained by limited dataset scale and insufficient coverages of cancer and chemical spaces. In addition, inconsistent benchmarking practices hinder reliable comparison across models. Standardized frameworks, such as the Innovative Methodologies and New Data for Predictive Oncology Model Evaluation (IMPROVE) project, provide unified data schemas and evaluation protocols for consistent benchmarking, but improving model generalizability requires larger and more diverse training data. In this work, we substantially expand the IMPROVE benchmark through large-scale integration of pharmacogenomic data, primarily from PharmacoDB, together with additional smaller data sources. The expanded resource includes millions of drug response measurements, broader multi-omics coverage, and a major increase in chemical diversity, adding more than 50,000 compounds. To evaluate the impact of the new dataset compared to the original IMPROVE benchmark dataset, we trained DRP models using the two datasets and assess their prediction performance using a common test set and several evaluation strategies, including drug-blind, cancer-blind, and disjoint data splits. While cancer-blind performance remained comparable to the original benchmark, models trained on the expanded dataset showed consistent improvements in drug-blind and disjoint settings, indicating enhanced generalization to previously unseen compounds. These results position the expanded dataset as a community resource that provides a richer foundation for developing DRP models intended to aid in the discovery of novel anticancer drugs.

AI.tldr: This paper expands the IMPROVE benchmark for drug response prediction by integrating large-scale pharmacogenomic data (primarily from PharmacoDB) with additional sources, adding millions of drug response measurements, broader multi-omics coverage, and over 50,000 new compounds. Models trained on the expanded dataset show improved generalization to unseen drugs (drug-blind and disjoint splits) while maintaining comparable cancer-blind performance, positioning it as a community resource for developing better DRP models.
AI.motivation: Drug response prediction models face performance constraints due to limited dataset scale and insufficient coverage of both cancer and chemical spaces, while inconsistent benchmarking practices hinder reliable model comparison across studies. Although standardized frameworks like IMPROVE provide unified evaluation protocols, improving model generalizability requires larger and more diverse training data.
AI.method: The authors substantially expand the IMPROVE benchmark through large-scale integration of pharmacogenomic data, primarily from PharmacoDB plus additional smaller data sources. They train DRP models on both the expanded and original datasets, evaluating prediction performance using a common test set with multiple evaluation strategies including drug-blind, cancer-blind, and disjoint data splits.
AI.result: The expanded dataset contains millions of drug response measurements, broader multi-omics coverage, and more than 50,000 additional compounds. Cancer-blind performance remained comparable to the original benchmark, but models trained on the expanded dataset showed consistent improvements in drug-blind and disjoint settings, indicating enhanced generalization to previously unseen compounds.
AI.conclusion: The expanded dataset serves as a community resource providing a richer foundation for developing DRP models intended to aid in the discovery of novel anticancer drugs, particularly by improving generalization to unseen chemical space.

title: Probing and steering biology across Boltz-1s trunk-diffusion boundary
summary: AlphaFold3-class structure predictors pair a representational trunk, which processes sequence and context, with a diffusion module, which generates atomic coordinates. How biological information changes as it crosses this architectural boundary remains poorly understood. We analyze per-residue activations from the Pairformer trunk and diffusion module of Boltz-1 using linear probes, sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and causal interventions. From the trunk, both geometry (secondary structure, disorder) and sequence chemistry (amino-acid identity, signal peptides, disulfide-bond annotations) are linearly decodable. In the diffusion module, the two diverge. Secondary structure transfers essentially unchanged, whereas sequence chemistry is strongly attenuated. We then test whether decodable directions can steer the model, intervening on the final trunk single representation that conditions the diffusion module. Helix and coil directions change predicted structure dose-dependently against matched-norm random controls, but a beta-strand direction that is highly predictive (F1 =0.82) produces no measurable increase in strand content: linear decodability does not imply causal influence at the site we tested. The same probes also score markedly lower against sparse SwissProt annotations than against dense DSSP labels, because unannotated residues that the model gets right are charged as false positives; such scores are therefore lower bounds. Finally, supervised probes outscore single SAE features wherever a label already exists. We release the trained trunk and diffusion SAEs, Boltz-1 per-residue activations, and the analysis code.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how biological information flows across the architectural boundary between the representational trunk and diffusion module in AlphaFold3-class structure predictors (specifically Boltz-1). Using linear probes, sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and causal interventions, the authors find that geometry (secondary structure, disorder) transfers largely unchanged to the diffusion module, while sequence chemistry is strongly attenuated. They also demonstrate that linear decodability does not imply causal influence, as highly predictive helix/coil directions could steer predictions but a highly predictive beta-strand direction could not.
AI.motivation: Understanding how biological information (sequence chemistry and structure geometry) is transformed as it crosses the architectural boundary between the trunk and diffusion module remains poorly understood. This has implications for interpretability, controllability, and trust in AlphaFold3-class structure predictors.
AI.method: The authors analyze per-residue activations from the Pairformer trunk and diffusion module of Boltz-1 using three complementary techniques: (1) linear probes to test decodability of geometric and chemical features, (2) sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to discover interpretable features, and (3) causal interventions on the final trunk single representation to test whether decodable directions can steer the model's predicted structure.
AI.result: (1) Both geometry and sequence chemistry are linearly decodable from the trunk, but in the diffusion module, secondary structure transfers while sequence chemistry is attenuated. (2) Helix and coil steering directions change predicted structure dose-dependently, but a highly predictive beta-strand direction (F1=0.82) produces no measurable effect, showing decodability does not imply causality. (3) Supervised probes score lower against sparse SwissProt annotations than dense DSSP labels due to false-positive charges on unannotated residues. (4) Supervised probes outperform single SAE features wherever labels exist.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals an asymmetric transfer of biological information across the trunk-diffusion boundary (structure geometry preserved, sequence chemistry attenuated) and cautions that linear decodability is not a reliable proxy for causal influence in these models. The authors release all trained models, activations, and analysis code for reproducibility.

title: Conflict and Congruency Effects in Large Language Models: In-Weight and In-Context Competition in a Verbal Conflict Task
summary: Congruency effects, observed in conflict tasks such as Stroop and flanker tasks, have been investigated for nearly a century in psychology and neuroscience, but their mechanistic basis is not fully understood. We introduce a verbal-only LLM conflict task in which a prompt stem elicits a default same-color completion and an explicit rule either agrees with (congruent condition) or conflicts with (incongruent condition) the completion. Gemma-2-2B and six Pythia models ranging from 410M to 12B parameters showed strong default same-color tendencies, and six of seven models showed strong congruency effects. Using causal attribution analysis, attention analysis, and attention ablations, we identified distinct processing pathways in these LLMs: a pathway involving short-range attention to a superficial color cue that is preferentially activated in the congruent condition, and a pathway involving long-range attention to the rule prefix that is preferentially activated in the incongruent condition. Fine-tuning that strengthened the default same-color tendency had divergent effects on task conditions, reducing incongruent performance while increasing congruent performance. In contrast, increasing rule set size selectively impaired incongruent performance. These converging findings support an account in which congruency effects in this task arise from competition between an in-weight default mapping and an in-context rule-based mapping. More broadly, our findings illustrate how LLMs can serve as model systems for mechanistic analysis of competition between default and rule-governed response tendencies within a single learned network.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a verbal-only LLM conflict task analogous to classic Stroop/flanker tasks, demonstrating that LLMs (Gemma-2-2B and six Pythia models) exhibit congruency effects, and uses causal attribution and attention analyses to identify distinct processing pathways for congruent (short-range color cue) versus incongruent (long-range rule prefix) conditions. Converging evidence from fine-tuning and rule set size manipulations supports competition between an in-weight default mapping and an in-context rule-based mapping.
AI.motivation: Congruency effects in conflict tasks (e.g., Stroop, flanker) have been studied for nearly a century, yet their mechanistic basis remains incompletely understood. The authors aim to leverage LLMs as model systems to mechanistically dissect the competition between default and rule-governed response tendencies within a single learned network.
AI.method: The authors designed a verbal-only conflict task where a prompt stem triggers a default same-color completion and an explicit rule either agrees (congruent) or conflicts (incongruent) with it. They tested Gemma-2-2B and six Pythia models (410M-12B), and applied causal attribution analysis, attention analysis, and attention ablations to identify neural pathways. They also performed fine-tuning to strengthen default same-color tendency and manipulated rule set size to observe effects on performance.
AI.result: All models showed strong default same-color tendencies, and six of seven showed strong congruency effects. A short-range attention pathway to a superficial color cue was preferentially activated in congruent conditions, while a long-range attention pathway to the rule prefix was activated in incongruent conditions. Strengthening the default tendency reduced incongruent performance but increased congruent performance, while increasing rule set size selectively impaired incongruent performance.
AI.conclusion: The findings support an account where congruency effects arise from competition between an in-weight default mapping and an in-context rule-based mapping. More broadly, LLMs can serve as model systems for mechanistic analysis of competition between default and rule-governed response tendencies within a single learned network.

title: SVPLEX: A Nextflow Pipeline for Cohort-level Structural Variant Calling
summary: SVPLEX is a Nextflow pipeline for cohort-level structural variant detection from short-read whole-genome sequencing data. The pipeline implements six different structural variant callers with different strengths and weaknesses, integrating different levels of evidence for SVs, and generates a merged consensus callset across the analysis cohort. Callset filtering is achieved by leveraging consensus among multiple individual callers and by ensuring that deletion and duplication calls are supported by observable changes in read depth. The output merged cohort SV callset can then be used to assess cohort-specific variation, remove technical artefacts, and serve as input for rare disease variant prioritisation workflows. SVPLEX is user-friendly, reproducible, scalable, and can be executed flexibly on either a local workstation, a high-performance compute (HPC) cluster, or deployed on cloud infrastructure. The required inputs are alignment files for the cohort of interest, and the output is a single merged cohort structural variant VCF. SVPLEX is available on GitHub (bahlolab/SVPLEX) and is licensed under the MIT open-source licence.

AI.tldr: SVPLEX is a Nextflow pipeline that detects structural variants (SVs) from short-read whole-genome sequencing data using six complementary SV callers, merges them into a consensus cohort-level callset, and filters calls through multi-caller consensus and read-depth evidence to produce a single merged VCF for downstream applications.
AI.motivation: Structural variant detection from short-read sequencing data is challenging due to inconsistent results across individual callers, requiring a cohort-level consensus approach to reduce technical artefacts and enable reliable SV analysis for population studies and rare disease prioritisation.
AI.method: The pipeline integrates six structural variant callers with different strengths, leverages consensus among multiple callers for filtering, ensures deletion/duplication calls are supported by read depth changes, and is implemented in Nextflow for scalable, reproducible execution across local, HPC, or cloud environments.
AI.result: SVPLEX produces a single merged cohort structural variant VCF requiring only alignment files as input, suitable for cohort-specific variation assessment, technical artefact removal, and rare disease variant prioritisation workflows.
AI.conclusion: SVPLEX provides a user-friendly, reproducible, and scalable solution for cohort-level structural variant detection accessible on GitHub under the MIT open-source licence.

title: A multiscale theory based on metabolic scaling connects forest dynamics to tree-size distributions
summary: Scaling relations linking species size, abundance, and resource availability are among the most robust empirical regularities in ecology. However, a mechanistic explanation for how these community-level laws emerge from ecological processes remains elusive. Here, we address this gap by developing a minimal spatially explicit dynamical framework for forest communities that incorporates seed dispersal, growth limited by local light availability, local competition, and global resource constraints grounded in metabolic scaling principles. By deriving an analytical solution for the tree-size distribution, we show that its stationary state exhibits two distinct power-law regimes whose exponents are controlled by the relative strength of resource and spatial competition. The crossover between these regimes is set by the interplay between seed injection and local resource availability, establishing an explicit link between the scaling exponent of the size distribution and forest condition. Finally, we show that boundary disturbances can break the ecological balance between competing species and induce effects that propagate deeply into the forest bulk, far beyond the single-plant dispersal range. Together, these results provide a unifying dynamical perspective on forest scaling laws with potential applications to a broad range of biological communities.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a minimal spatially explicit dynamical framework for forest communities that incorporates seed dispersal, light-limited growth, local competition, and global resource constraints based on metabolic scaling. The authors derive an analytical solution for the tree-size distribution showing two distinct power-law regimes controlled by the relative strength of resource versus spatial competition, and demonstrate that boundary disturbances can propagate effects deep into the forest bulk.
AI.motivation: Scaling relations linking species size, abundance, and resource availability are among the most robust empirical regularities in ecology, yet a mechanistic explanation for how these community-level laws emerge from underlying ecological processes has been missing. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a dynamical framework that explains how these scaling laws arise.
AI.method: The authors develop a minimal spatially explicit dynamical framework for forest communities incorporating four key processes: seed dispersal, growth limited by local light availability, local competition, and global resource constraints grounded in metabolic scaling principles. They derive an analytical solution for the tree-size distribution and examine its stationary state.
AI.result: The stationary tree-size distribution exhibits two distinct power-law regimes whose exponents are controlled by the relative strength of resource versus spatial competition. The crossover between regimes is determined by the interplay between seed injection and local resource availability, linking the scaling exponent to forest condition. Additionally, boundary disturbances can break ecological balance between competing species and induce effects propagating far into the forest bulk beyond the single-plant dispersal range.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a unifying dynamical perspective on forest scaling laws with potential applications to a broad range of biological communities, establishing an explicit mechanism connecting ecological processes to community-level scaling regularities.

title: Beyond Local Power: Functional Connectivity Analysis for Subject-Independent Learning Style Recognition
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication at 4th IEEE International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Mechatronics Systems 2026
summary: Identifying individual learning styles optimizes pedagogical efficacy. While traditional questionnaires are structured, behavioral tracking methods require prolonged interaction log accumulation. To overcome these temporal constraints, this paper proposes an objective Electroencephalography (EEG) approach evaluating Phase Locking Value (PLV) connectivity against localized features across the Active-Reflective (AR) and Verbal-Visual (VV) Felder-Silverman dimensions. EEG signals were recorded from 28 participants during Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices tasks. Support Vector Machine classification used Leave-One-Subject-Out Cross-Validation (LOSO-CV) alongside a 70:30 intra-subject split. The VV dimension achieved 70.00% subject-level accuracy driven by distinct fronto-occipital polarization. Conversely, the AR dimension yielded lower cross-subject generalizability (55.56%) due to overlapping executive networks and a "Systematic Neural Inversion" phenomenon, where stable individual connectivity signatures operated diametrically opposed to global boundaries (up to 20-0 voting margins). Ultimately, these outcomes demonstrate that rigid "one-size-fits-all" classifiers are bounded by biological diversity, emphasizing the need for future adaptive feature transformation techniques to bridge the cross-subject generalization gap.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an EEG-based approach to identify learning styles using Phase Locking Value (PLV) connectivity across Active-Reflective and Verbal-Visual Felder-Silverman dimensions. VV achieved 70% subject-level accuracy via fronto-occipital polarization, while AR showed only 55.56% cross-subject accuracy due to overlapping executive networks and a "Systematic Neural Inversion" phenomenon, highlighting limits of one-size-fits-all classifiers.
AI.motivation: Traditional learning style assessments rely on questionnaires or prolonged behavioral tracking, both of which are temporally constrained. The authors aim to overcome these limitations by proposing an objective EEG-based approach that can assess learning styles more rapidly.
AI.method: EEG signals were recorded from 28 participants during Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices tasks. Phase Locking Value (PLV) connectivity was evaluated against localized features across Active-Reflective (AR) and Verbal-Visual (VV) dimensions. Support Vector Machine classification was employed with both Leave-One-Subject-Out Cross-Validation (LOSO-CV) and a 70:30 intra-subject split.
AI.result: The VV dimension achieved 70.00% subject-level accuracy driven by distinct fronto-occipital polarization. The AR dimension yielded only 55.56% cross-subject generalizability due to overlapping executive networks and a "Systematic Neural Inversion" phenomenon, where stable individual connectivity signatures operated in opposite directions to global boundaries (voting margins up to 20-0).
AI.conclusion: Rigid "one-size-fits-all" classifiers are bounded by biological diversity. Future work requires adaptive feature transformation techniques to bridge the cross-subject generalization gap in EEG-based learning style classification.

title: The Rosetta Stone and Levels of Principled Inference to the Experience of Another Mind
comment: To appear in Qualia Structure. Springer Nature (forthcoming)
summary: The classical problem of Other Minds has dogged philosophers for millennia; asking if we have any way to truly understand the experience of another mind. We know our own intrinsic experience by acquaintance, but can only ever hope to possess an extrinsic description of another's, with the two separated by an acquaintance gap. Structural approaches aim to characterise experience in terms of a mathematical structure, and promise a 'Rosetta Stone'; that is, a principled method to translate the contents of experience into a mathematical structure. In this chapter, we examine two such approaches - the Qualia Structure Paradigm (Qstr) and Integrated Information Theory (IIT) - to ask what, if anything, they allow us to infer about another mind should they possess the Rosetta Stone they seek. Qstr proceeds inter-phenomenally; aiming to exhaustively characterise an experience by its relations to all other experiences and providing a necessary condition on the sameness of experience. IIT proceeds intra-phenomenally; conjecturing that a single experience is accounted for by the cause-effect structure unfolded from a substrate in a state, an explanatory identity that is both necessary and sufficient for the sameness of experience. While neither approach can cross the acquaintance gap to another's mind, they provide a common formal medium through which minds may be compared and in turn reduce the size of this gap. We identify the strength of inference with levels of structural correspondence in Category Theory. These descend from isomorphism through strong and weak adjunction, to a principled limit where inference runs out. We conclude that these structural approaches and the existence of their respective Rosetta Stones would not solve the problem of Other Minds, but instead provide a system of principled constraints on what we may infer, which is far more than what has been justifiable before.

AI.tldr: This chapter examines two structural approaches to consciousness—the Qualia Structure Paradigm (Qstr) and Integrated Information Theory (IIT)—to assess what they allow us to infer about another mind. While neither can fully cross the "acquaintance gap" between our own experience and another's, they provide a common formal medium (Category Theory) for comparing minds, reducing—though not eliminating—the gap. The strength of inference is graded by levels of structural correspondence (isomorphism, adjunction, etc.), yielding principled constraints on what we can justifiably infer about other minds.
AI.motivation: The classical "Other Minds" problem asks whether we can ever truly understand another's experience. Structural approaches to consciousness—which characterize experience in mathematical terms—promise a "Rosetta Stone" for translating experience into structure. This paper asks whether such approaches, if successful, would actually allow us to infer anything about other minds, and how strong any such inference could be.
AI.method: The authors analyze and compare two structural frameworks: (1) Qstr, which proceeds inter-phenomenally by characterizing an experience through its relations to all other experiences, providing a necessary condition on sameness of experience; and (2) IIT, which proceeds intra-phenomenally by positing that a single experience corresponds to the cause-effect structure of a substrate, providing an explanatory identity that is both necessary and sufficient. They formalize the strength of inference across the acquaintance gap using Category Theory, grading levels of structural correspondence from isomorphism through strong/weak adjunction down to a principled limit where inference ceases.
AI.result: Neither Qstr nor IIT can cross the acquaintance gap to truly access another mind's experience. However, both provide a common formal medium for comparing minds, which reduces the size of the gap. The authors identify graded levels of structural correspondence (in Category Theory) that determine how strongly one may infer about another mind, establishing a principled boundary where inference runs out.
AI.conclusion: Structural approaches to consciousness and their promised "Rosetta Stones" would not solve the problem of Other Minds outright. Instead, they would provide a system of principled constraints on what may be inferred about other minds—a significant advance over what has been justifiable before, though falling short of full access to another's subjective experience.

title: Dynamics of fluctuating populations in multi-state switching environments
comment: 13-page main text + 7-page appendix, 8+2 figures. Simulation data and codes are electronically available from the University of Leeds Data Repository: https://doi.org/10.5518/1899
summary: Microbial populations generally evolve in fluctuating environments under time-varying conditions. These are often described by binary switching models, sometimes seen as coarse-grained feast-famine cycles, in which resource availability switches abruptly between abundant and scarce conditions. However, experimental studies suggest that feast-famine environments actually exhibit more complex temporal dynamics. Here, we study how two strains, one growing slightly slower than the other, compete for the same resources in fluctuating environments comprising a finite number of intermediate states, each having its own carrying capacity. Environmental switching between these states and their carrying capacities represents gradual changes in nutrient availability. This class of multi-state stochastic switching models can be interpreted as a coarse-grained description of feast--famine cycles and allows us to investigate strain competition under the gradual recovery and depletion of resources. By computational and analytical means, we characterise the population dynamics in these multi-state fluctuating environments. In particular, we study how the switching rates and distribution of carrying capacities affect the population-size statistics, fixation probability, and mean fixation time. By comparing these results with their counterparts in binary environments, we clarify how the frequency and amplitude of environmental fluctuations influence population dynamics in coarse-grained feast-famine cycles.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how two competing microbial strains evolve in multi-state fluctuating environments, which serve as coarse-grained models of feast-famine cycles. Unlike binary switching models, this model includes finite intermediate states with distinct carrying capacities, capturing gradual resource depletion and recovery. The authors characterize population dynamics both computationally and analytically, examining how switching rates and carrying capacity distributions affect population-size statistics, fixation probability, and mean fixation time, and compare these to binary environment results.
AI.motivation: Real feast-famine environments exhibit complex temporal dynamics beyond simple binary switching between abundant and scarce conditions. Existing binary switching models are too coarse to capture gradual changes in nutrient availability, so a more realistic multi-state framework is needed to understand strain competition in fluctuating environments.
AI.method: The authors develop a multi-state stochastic switching model where environments transition among a finite number of intermediate states, each with its own carrying capacity. They use both computational simulations and analytical methods to characterize population dynamics, fixation probability, and mean fixation time under varying switching rates and carrying capacity distributions.
AI.result: The study characterizes population dynamics in multi-state fluctuating environments, revealing how switching rates and carrying capacity distributions influence population-size statistics, fixation probability, and mean fixation time. Comparisons with binary environments clarify the role of fluctuation frequency and amplitude in coarse-grained feast-famine cycles.
AI.conclusion: Multi-state fluctuating environments provide a more realistic description of feast-famine cycles than binary switching models, and the frequency and amplitude of environmental fluctuations have important effects on strain competition dynamics that differ from binary environment predictions.

title: A Modular Agentic Framework for Synthetically Constrained Multi-Objective Hit-to-Lead Optimization
summary: Hit-to-lead optimization requires iterative design of hit analogs across competing potency, selectivity, physicochemical, pharmacokinetic, safety, and synthetic constraints. We present SABLE (Synthetically-accessible Agentic Bayesian Ligand Exploration), an open-source framework that employs natural-language orchestration to guide chemical structure optimization. SABLE uses an LLM to interpret user-defined goals and route tasks, while specialized tools perform reaction-templated analog enumeration, physicochemical and ADMET property prediction, structure-based affinity scoring, and Bayesian optimization. The resulting workflow is a computational twin of the analytical and prioritization stages of the design-make-test-analyze cycle, providing provenance of each numerical output. Across single, and multi-objective optimization studies, SABLE enriches candidate sets for user-defined computational objectives while evaluating only a subset of the enumerated search space. Its modular architecture allows tools and characterization backends to be replaced by editing a simple config file, without modifying operational logic. SABLE provides an extensible decision-support framework for prioritizing synthetically constrained analogs in early-stage drug discovery.

AI.tldr: SABLE is an open-source, natural-language-orchestrated framework for hit-to-lead optimization in drug discovery. It uses an LLM to interpret user goals and coordinate specialized tools (reaction-templated analog enumeration, ADMET prediction, structure-based affinity scoring, Bayesian optimization), acting as a computational twin of the design-make-test-analyze cycle with full provenance tracking. It enriches candidate sets across single and multi-objective studies while evaluating only a subset of the search space, and features modular architecture where tools can be swapped via config files without changing operational logic.
AI.motivation: Hit-to-lead optimization requires iterative analog design balancing competing constraints (potency, selectivity, physicochemical properties, PK, safety, and synthetic accessibility). Existing workflows lack a unified, extensible framework that can integrate these heterogeneous objectives with provenance and natural-language-driven orchestration.
AI.method: SABLE combines an LLM orchestrator (parsing user goals and routing tasks) with specialized tools: reaction-templated analog enumeration, physicochemical and ADMET property prediction, structure-based affinity scoring, and Bayesian optimization. The workflow mirrors the design-make-test-analyze cycle, with a modular config-file-driven architecture that allows backend/tool replacement without altering core logic.
AI.result: In single and multi-objective optimization studies, SABLE enriches candidate sets for user-defined computational objectives while evaluating only a subset of the enumerated search space, demonstrating efficiency and effectiveness in prioritizing synthetically constrained analogs.
AI.conclusion: SABLE provides an extensible decision-support framework for prioritizing synthetically constrained analogs in early-stage drug discovery, offering a flexible and provenance-rich alternative to traditional hit-to-lead optimization pipelines.

title: Testing the limits of past-adapted explanations by post-endpoint randomisation: anticipatory EEG as a worked case
comment: Perspective article. 90 pages, 6 figures, 15 tables; includes Supplementary Information. No human EEG data are analysed. Synthetic benchmark and reproducible software are available at https://github.com/geosop/LEVEL-IIA and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21887583
summary: A predictive model can fit its data even when its information set is insufficient; fit alone cannot establish sufficiency. This Perspective introduces Level II-A, a new design-based inference framework to test this distinction, illustrated in anticipatory EEG using contingent negative variation. A pre-event endpoint is committed before the delay to the imperative event is randomised. That later-assigned delay thereby becomes a negative-control probe of whether past-adapted information was sufficient for an already committed result. Under the past-adapted factorisation, accounts using only pre-commitment information cannot systematically order the endpoint by that delay. Leakage-safe preprocessing, a frozen label-blind comparator and retained-sample qualifications carry the exclusion to the confirmatory residual. A qualified material negative ordering supports conditional insufficiency without identifying a mechanism; an adequately sensitive null supports a bounded affirmative conclusion calibrated by the pipeline's false-adequacy rate. A non-compensatory rule separates these from diagnostic failure, selection-limited, opposite-direction and inconclusive outcomes. No human EEG data are analysed. In the synthetic benchmark, grid-based false-adequacy boundaries are $15\,μ\mathrm{V\,s^{-1}}$ for assignment isolation and $30\,μ\mathrm{V\,s^{-1}}$ for the sequential e-value route, in both directions. The design transfers wherever endpoint commitment precedes an exogenous label, probing sufficiency only where a declared alternative predicts ordering by it. It turns "the past explains it" from a working explanatory assumption into a magnitude-qualified, testable claim.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Level II-A, a design-based inference framework for testing whether a predictive model's fit is sufficient (as opposed to merely necessary) given its information set. Using anticipatory EEG contingent negative variation as an illustrative case, the framework leverages a pre-event endpoint committed before delay randomization, making the later-assigned delay a negative-control probe. It provides leakage-safe preprocessing, a frozen label-blind comparator, and a non-compensatory decision rule to distinguish conditional insufficiency from other outcomes, with synthetic benchmarks establishing false-adequacy boundaries.
AI.motivation: A predictive model can fit its data even when its information set is insufficient—fit alone cannot establish sufficiency. The authors aim to distinguish between "the past explains it" as a working assumption versus a testable claim by introducing a rigorous inference framework.
AI.method: The framework commits a pre-event endpoint before the delay to the imperative event is randomized, turning the later-assigned delay into a negative-control probe. Under the past-adapted factorization, models using only pre-commitment information cannot systematically order the endpoint by that delay. The method employs leakage-safe preprocessing, a frozen label-blind comparator, and retained-sample qualifications to carry the exclusion to the confirmatory residual. A non-compensatory rule categorizes outcomes including conditional insufficiency, bounded affirmative conclusions, diagnostic failure, selection-limited, opposite-direction, and inconclusive cases.
AI.result: No human EEG data are analyzed. In synthetic benchmarks, grid-based false-adequacy boundaries are 15 μV·s⁻¹ for assignment isolation and 30 μV·s⁻¹ for the sequential e-value route, in both directions.
AI.conclusion: The design transfers wherever endpoint commitment precedes an exogenous label, probing sufficiency only where a declared alternative predicts ordering by it. It converts "the past explains it" from a working explanatory assumption into a magnitude-qualified, testable claim.

title: Task- and dataset-specific information in protein language models
summary: Protein language models (PLMs) have transferred the latest advances from natural language processing to computational biology. These models, trained on large corpora of protein sequence data, are widely used to translate amino acid sequences into latent-space embeddings, ready for use in diverse downstream tasks (DTs). By a common consensus, embeddings from the model's last layer are used, and the model's internal behavior remains poorly understood. We analyzed 13 PLMs across 15 DTs from 11 datasets to investigate the informativeness of embeddings created in intermediate PLM layers. We trained probe models on embeddings from each layer, compared their performance, and computed characteristics of the latent spaces they span to estimate the information they contain, and found that the last layers of PLMs rarely contained embeddings that led to the best results on downstream tasks. Furthermore, we identified a connection between DTs and the distribution across PLMs' layers of the relevant information to predict that task. For example, similarity between the pre-training objective and the objective of predicting properties of individual residues leads to a steady increase in understanding of such tasks across the layers of PLMs. On the other hand, for whole-protein tasks, we observe that the dataset, rather than the task itself, defines PLMs' ability to perform well on a DT. Embeddings from shallow layers of PLMs perform better for datasets that contain deep mutational scan (DMS) data, while datasets containing diverse natural proteins find most useful embeddings in the models' deeper layers. Additionally, we discover that the performance of PLMs drops significantly when tasks are introduced for artificial proteins.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically analyzes 13 protein language models (PLMs) across 15 downstream tasks from 11 datasets, examining the informativeness of embeddings from intermediate layers. Contrary to common practice of using last-layer embeddings, the authors find that last layers rarely yield the best results. They identify connections between task types and optimal layer depths, showing that residue-level tasks benefit from progressively deeper layers, while whole-protein tasks' performance depends more on dataset characteristics than task type. Performance drops significantly for artificial proteins.
AI.motivation: Despite the widespread adoption of PLMs in computational biology, their internal behavior remains poorly understood. The common practice is to use embeddings from the final layer for downstream tasks without a principled understanding of which layers contain the most relevant information. This work aims to systematically investigate intermediate layer embeddings across many models and tasks to understand where task-relevant information resides in PLMs.
AI.method: The authors analyze 13 PLMs across 15 downstream tasks from 11 datasets. They train probe models on embeddings extracted from each layer of each PLM, compare their performance across layers, and compute characteristics of the latent spaces they span to estimate information content. They examine relationships between downstream task types, dataset properties (including DMS data vs. diverse natural proteins vs. artificial proteins), and the layer distribution of predictive information.
AI.result: Last-layer PLM embeddings rarely produce the best downstream task performance. A connection exists between task types and where relevant information resides across layers: residue-level property prediction tasks show monotonic improvement across layers (aligned with the pre-training objective), while whole-protein tasks' performance is driven more by dataset characteristics than the task itself—shallow layers work better for DMS datasets, deeper layers for diverse natural protein datasets, and performance drops significantly on artificial proteins.
AI.conclusion: The common assumption that last-layer embeddings are optimal for all downstream tasks is incorrect. The optimal layer depth depends on both the task type and the dataset characteristics. This suggests that practitioners should select layers more carefully based on their specific task and data, and that PLM internal representations should be better understood to improve downstream performance.

title: On the Convergence Rate Lower Bound of Biochemical Computational Modules
summary: Biochemical reaction networks have become a central theoretical framework for implementing molecular computation. A key challenge is finite time computational accuracy, as computation outputs are encoded in limiting steady states (LSSs) of species concentrations while practical implementations operate for only finite time. This work proposes a concise characterization of convergence rate for biochemical computational modules with multiple output species, and rigorously establishes it as being bounded by the eigenvalue with largest (least negative) real part of the Jacobian matrix. Two numerical examples illustrate how the theoretical lower bound shapes the convergence rate range and reveals its dependence on reaction rate constants. This formulation enables systematic evaluation of biochemical computation speed and provides a practical design measure for constructing high-accuracy and error-controlled biochemical computational modules.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a characterization of convergence rate for biochemical reaction network computations with multiple output species, proving that the convergence rate is bounded by the eigenvalue with the largest (least negative) real part of the Jacobian matrix, and demonstrates this via numerical examples.
AI.motivation: Biochemical reaction networks are used for molecular computation, but practical implementations operate only for finite time while computation outputs are encoded in limiting steady states (LSSs). This creates a key challenge of finite-time computational accuracy, motivating the need to characterize and understand convergence rates.
AI.method: The paper derives a concise characterization of the convergence rate for biochemical computational modules with multiple output species, rigorously establishing that this rate is bounded by the eigenvalue with the largest (least negative) real part of the Jacobian matrix. Two numerical examples are used to illustrate how the theoretical lower bound shapes the convergence rate range.
AI.result: The theoretical lower bound (governed by the least negative eigenvalue of the Jacobian) shapes the convergence rate range, and the analysis reveals the dependence of convergence speed on reaction rate constants through numerical examples.
AI.conclusion: The proposed formulation enables systematic evaluation of biochemical computation speed and provides a practical design measure for constructing high-accuracy and error-controlled biochemical computational modules.
